thread.title: Alphabet: Hardly Matters - Alphabet, Inc. Cl A (NASDAQ:GOOGL) | Seeking Alpha

author: Stone Fox Capital
title: Alphabet: Hardly Matters - Alphabet, Inc. Cl A (NASDAQ:GOOGL) | Seeking Alpha
text:
As other tech giants make the move to high-margin services, Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ) continues making the odd shift into hardware. A big part of the move is to lock consumers into their services and advertising revenue streams. The stock remains incredibly cheap back below $1,000 as highlighted in my previous research , but the push into hardware isn't likely to contribute to this valuation.
Image Source: Alphabet website
Other Revenues, Not Bets Alphabet has slowly moved into hardware for years now. The company has the Pixel smartphone, Nest thermostat and Home smart speaker, among other products. None of these items generate market-moving revenue and profits. And services like cloud and the potential for robotaxis via Waymo are likely to be the more important drivers of any non-advertising business.
For starters, it's important to understand the revenue streams of the different business lines of the tech giant. Alphabet gets the vast majority of revenue from the Google advertising business. In Q3, ad revenues were almost $29 billion and accounted for 85.8% of revenues. Google other revenues were $4.6 billion for 13.8% of revenues while Other Bets were a tiny fraction of total revenues at only $146 million.
Source: Alphabet Q3'18 10-Q
The key here is that the Other revenues category includes cloud revenues and Google Play in-app purchases so the category is a mixture of hardware and services. Another important distinction is that Waymo falls into the Other Bets category and recently started robotaxi services in the Phoenix area.
The problem with hardware is that it generates forecasted gross margins that hardly top the operating margins of the ad business. In Q3, Alphabet had Q3 gross margins at 60%.
Mark Mahaney of RBC Capital plugged the Google hardware business at nearly $20 billion by 2021 ( via CNBC). The amount sounds impressive until realizing the ad business alone will top $100 billion this year.
Source: RBC Capital
Mahaney sees the big growth drivers in the hardware business coming from Pixel smartphones and Home smart speakers. Anybody just needs to look at the iPhone business from Apple ( AAPL ) to understand the opportunity in this category.
The iPhone generated $166.7 billion in FY18 revenues ending in September. One naturally understands why Google would make an attempt to produce a competitive smartphone, but RBC only sees Pixel revenues reaching $6.9 billion by 2021.
The other reason is that Apple will collect up to $9 billion in fees for making Google the default search engine for iOS products. Google would prefer to reduce that payment going forward by having consumers bypass the iPhone for a Pixel.
Minimal Hardware Profits Even with a projection of hardware revenues of $19.6 billion in 2021, RBC projects a gross profit of only $6.1 billion. The more stunning number might be the target for hardware gross profits to only reach 5% of the company total. In essence, RBC is saying that hardware-specific revenues won't matter at this rate.
Source: RBC Capital
The most interesting story here is the smart speakers where RBC forecasts revenues of $8.2 billion. Here again, RBC has an aggressive forecast for revenues, especially if the amount is only hardware related. Remember that smart speakers are about capturing ad revenues from voice assistants.
Alphabet competes against market leader Amazon ( AMZN ) in this category and notably the online retail giant isn't about maximizing profits. As well, the market hasn't shown the expected level of consumer demand with the category focused on speakers actually turning into a way to listen to music.
eMarketer ( via TechCrunch ) places the shopping and buying functions down the list of importance. Both Amazon and Google wanted consumers to search for products via these voice-assisted services, but the average consumer hasn't been following due to data privacy issues. Both Apple ( AAPL ) and Sonos ( SONO ) have had recent success from focusing more on the audio aspect of smart speakers that might ultimately limit the market share of Google.
The market research firm suggests that voice commerce will only amount to about $2 billion in revenues. The percentage of consumers buying with this voice service is actually expected to drop from 31% to only 27%. The vast majority of consumers will use smart speakers as an actual speaker.
The revenue estimates of RBC appear a huge stretch. To reach $8 billion in sales by 2021, Google would have to sell more than 80 million Home products a year. For the holidays, the Home Mini is on sale for only $29 so Google may only average $50 a Home product. To reach $8 billion in annual sales at these reduced prices, the company would have to sell 140 million smart speakers a year.
The rub in focusing on the hardware division of is that the division isn't going to contribute on the bottom line. Even Mahaney forecasts the Home division only generating gross profits of 25%.
The hardware division is a necessary evil to ensure Alphabet is positioned to combat any market shift toward a solution that would reduce search revenues from Google. The division just isn't a profit generator for the tech giant no matter how much the company tries.
Crazy Cheap Over a year ago, my article focused on Alphabet deserving to trade above $1,000. After this massive market selloff, the stock is down roughly $300 from the highs to $991.
On a GAAP basis, Alphabet now trades at about 21x forward EPS estimates. The stock trades at the lowest multiple of the last year.
GOOGL data by YCharts My issue with the GAAP numbers is that stock-based compensation or SBC is included in those numbers. My previous estimate is that Alphabet will earn ~$63 per share.
The company has about $102 billion in net cash or the equivalent of $145 per share. The enterprise value trades at about 13.4x those EPS estimates. The valuation multiple is incredibly low for a company that has consistently grown revenues in excess of 20% this decade.
Takeaway The key investor takeaway is that RBC overplays the financial impact of the hardware division. Alphabet might generate large revenue growth for the division, but the gross profits just aren't material for the business.
Alphabet remains a strong buy due to the large profits generated by the ad business and the potential in Cloud and Waymo. The stock is a gift back below $1,000. Alphabet should easily trade at an EV of 20x my EPS estimates of $63 for a price target in excess of $1,400 when considering the $145 in cash.
